questions.q: Computing (0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩) ⊗ |0⟩ with np.kron gives [0.6, 0, 0.8, 0]. Why is there a 0 between the 0.6 and the 0.8?
options: Because the second vector is |0⟩=[1,0], so each entry of the first vector gets multiplied by 1 then by 0, placing a 0 immediately after each nonzero entry from the first vector
Because the tensor product always alternates nonzero and zero entries regardless of the input vectors
This is a computational error -- the correct result should have no zeros at all
Because 0.6 and 0.8 do not sum to 1
questions.explain: Each entry of the first vector gets multiplied by every entry of the second vector [1,0] in order, so 0.6*1, 0.6*0, 0.8*1, 0.8*0 gives [0.6, 0, 0.8, 0] -- the zero appears because |0> itself has a 0 in its second position.

questions.q: Building |101⟩ by chaining two tensor products (|1⟩⊗|0⟩, then that result ⊗|1⟩) gives a single 1 at index 5 of an 8-dimensional vector. Why index 5 specifically?
options: Index 5 is arbitrary and would be different if you computed the tensor products in a different order
Because the binary number 101 equals the decimal number 5, and the standard basis ordering places the |101⟩ state at the position matching its binary value
Because there are exactly 5 total 1s and 0s in the state label "101"
Because 3 qubits always produce exactly 5 meaningful basis states
questions.explain: The standard basis ordering for n qubits places each computational basis state at the index equal to its binary value interpreted as a number -- 101 in binary is 5, so |101> has its single 1 at index 5 of the 8-dimensional (2^3) vector.

questions.q: Testing [1/√3, 1/√3, 1/√3, 0] against the [ac,ad,bc,bd] pattern, the 'b=0' branch fails because bc would have to be 0, but the equation requires bc=1/√3. What does this prove about the state?
options: It proves the state was not correctly normalized to begin with
Combined with the 'd=0' branch also failing, this proves NO choice of a,b,c,d can reproduce the state, meaning it is entangled
It proves the state is definitely a product state
It proves only that b cannot equal zero, with no further conclusion possible
questions.explain: Since bd=0 forces b=0 or d=0, and BOTH branches lead to a contradiction with a required nonzero value, there is no valid choice of a,b,c,d at all -- which is exactly the definition of an entangled state.

questions.q: Applying X⊗I to |01⟩ gives |11⟩. What does the tensor structure 'X⊗I' mean physically?
options: Apply the X gate only if both qubits are currently in state |1⟩
Apply the X gate to both qubits simultaneously
Apply the X gate to the first qubit while leaving the second qubit completely unchanged
Apply the identity gate to both qubits, with X having no actual effect
questions.explain: In a tensor product of gates, each factor acts on its corresponding qubit -- X acts on the first qubit (flipping it), while I (identity) leaves the second qubit exactly as it was.

questions.q: Why does X⊗I applied to |01⟩ give |11⟩ rather than |10⟩?
options: Because the tensor product operation always produces |11⟩ regardless of the input state
Because |11⟩ and |10⟩ are actually the same state in this basis
Because X acts on the FIRST qubit (flipping its 0 to a 1), while the second qubit's original value (1) is left untouched by the identity factor, so |01⟩ becomes |11⟩, not a flip of the second qubit
Because X⊗I secretly swaps the order of the two qubits during application
questions.explain: X⊗I only flips the first qubit (0→1) and leaves the second qubit's value (1) unchanged, turning |01⟩ into |11⟩ -- getting |10⟩ instead would require the gate ordering I⊗X, acting on the second qubit instead.
